newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece urged to make more progress on EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: Greece urged to make more progress on EMU criteria.

text.p: Greece, the only EU country yet to fulfill a single Maastricht criterion, has made progress towards EU convergence but still risks low growth and high debt to GDP ratio, said a senior economist at Salomon Brothers.
"Greece has made strides but risks staying in a cycle of low growth rates and high debt to GDP ratio," economist Miranda Xafa told a conference on the Greek economy organised by the Economist.
Fiscal adjustment will be the single, most important criterion for European Union convergence in the medium-term, said Xafa, who was a senior economic advisor to a 1990-93 conservative government.

Greece slashed its general government budget deficit in line with its revised 1994-99 convergence plan but this was mostly due to the restructuring of Greece's pension and social insurance funds system that was introduced in 1992, she said.
"The central government budget deficit to GDP ratio overshot the target by about 1.0 percent in 1996," said Xafa. "The social insurance surpluses will be exhausted in a few years."
Greece's general government budget deficit fell to 7.4 percent of GDP in 1996 from 9.1 percent in 1995 and is projected to drop further to 4.2 percent in 1997.
Figures show public debt increased more than the cumulative budget deficits of the last 17 years and the public debt to GDP ratio remains very high, she said.

The state continues to guarantee loans by public utilities that are not being serviced, therefore adding to the public debt without showing up in the budget, said Xafa in explaining why the public debt rose more than cumulative deficits.
The Salomon Brothers economist was also critical of profitable public utilities such as telecom OTE and the Public Power Corporation (DEH), saying they owed their profits to their monopoly status.

"DEH owes more than 1.0 trillion drachmas but threatens us with a black-out in the summer if we use air-conditioning," she said. "It is not clear whether OTE's profits go for investment and not for wage rises."
Xafa said excessive wage growth hurt the competitiveness of the economy and the current account deficit which is expected to widen to $4.6 billion in 1996 from about $3.0 billion in 1995.
"Greece is losing on competitiveness not because of the hard drachma policy but because of excessive wage demands," she said.
The real effective exchange rate of the drachma -- using both relative unit labour costs and GDP deflator as proxies -- has been rising since 1994, pointing to a loss of competitiveness, she said.

Xafa applauded the government for resisting demands by various special interest groups, introducing fixed coupon bonds and taking hesitant steps towards privatising some state-run companies and utilities.
